12 When must an object be in equilibrium?
A
when no resultant force acts on the object
B
when no resultant force and no resultant torque act on the object
C
when no resultant torque acts on the object
D
when the upward force on the object is equal and opposite to its weight

hints: Notice the word must in the stem - it asks for the condition that guarantees equilibrium in all cases.
Recall that resultant force controls translational motion and resultant torque controls rotational motion.
Think of a steering-wheel couple where opposite forces cancel to zero resultant force but still produce turning - what extra condition would rule this out?
walkthrough: Identify what equilibrium means for an extended object: no change in translational motion and no change in rotational motion.
Translate this into two physics conditions: vector sum of forces $\sum F = 0$ so there is no resultant force, and sum of moments about any point $\sum M = 0$ so there is no resultant torque.
Check why one condition alone is not enough: a couple can have zero resultant force yet still turn, and a single unbalanced force can have zero torque about one point yet still accelerate the mass.
Check the upward-force-equals-weight idea: it only balances vertical forces and says nothing about horizontal forces or about where the forces act and the torque they produce.
Only the statement requiring both no resultant force and no resultant torque guarantees both types of equilibrium. This is option B.

A.explanation: Zero resultant force stops linear acceleration but the object could still rotate if a couple gives a resultant torque.

B.explanation: Full equilibrium needs both no resultant force for no translation and no resultant torque for no rotation.

C.explanation: Zero resultant torque stops angular acceleration but the object could still accelerate linearly if a resultant force remains.

D.explanation: Balancing weight with an upward force ignores other horizontal forces and ignores torque that could still cause rotation.
